standing_assumptions:
The article is Carlson, Incerti and Aronow, ‘Dyadic Clustering in International Relations’, Political Analysis 32:186–198 (2024). Printed page = PDF page + 185 (printed p. 191 is PDF p. 6). Everything quoted below and in the targets was read from the rendered page images (staged/pages/p-NN.png and the publisher-supplement page images, checked against 170–220 dpi renderings of staged/main.pdf and of the supplement). The paper has no numbered theorem, proposition, lemma or equation; its formal content is two displays in Section 2.1, the sandwich displays and the decomposition display in Section 3, and Tables 2–4. It writes $\mathrm{V}[\cdot]$ for variance, $\mathrm{E}[\cdot]$ for expectation and a superscript $T$ for transpose.
(S1) Model, p. 189 (PDF p. 4), Section 3: “To ease exposition, we consider the linear model of $Y_{ijt}$ on regressors $x_{ijt}$, $$Y_{ijt} = \beta x_{ijt} + u_{ijt},$$ where $Y_{ijt}$ is the level of commerce between countries $i$ and $j$ in time period or observation $t$ and $\beta$ is the slope that we obtain from fitting this model to the entire population. Under the exogeneity condition $\mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}\,|\,x_{ijt}] = 0$ and the usual regularity conditions, the parameters of this model can be estimated using ordinary least squares.”
(S2) Sandwich and plug-in estimator, p. 189: “Generically, the variance of an estimated parameter from a linear model can be represented in a symmetric form that resembles a sandwich, with two identical “bread” matrices and a “meat” matrix multiplied together in the order of bread, meat, and bread again (Aronow and Miller 2019; Davidson and MacKinnon 2004; Greene 2002): $$V_{sandwich} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\Omega X(X^TX)^{-1},$$ where $X$ denotes the matrix of regressors, and $\Omega$ is the variance–covariance matrix of model errors, such that $\Omega_{ijt,i'j't'} = \mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}u_{i'j't'}]$. Robust sandwich estimators are formed by assuming that some elements of $\Omega$ are equal to zero, and then substituting residuals for errors, and means for expectations. Thus, the empirical variance–covariance matrix of model residuals, $\hat\Omega$, can be plugged into the above expression of variance to arrive at a variance estimator of the following form:$^1$ $$\hat V = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\hat\Omega X(X^TX)^{-1}.$$ So long as there is not “too much” clustering (for a precise statement, see Aronow, Crawford, and Zubizarreta 2018), $\hat V$ will be a consistent estimator of the variance–covariance matrix of the sampling distribution of $\hat\beta$.” Footnote 1: “Both the Eicker–Huber–White heteroskedasticity-consistent variance estimator and the Liang and Zeger cluster robust variance estimator are sandwich-like, “plug-in” variance estimators of this form, each making differing assumptions about $\Omega$.”
(S3) The three restrictions on $\Omega$, pp. 189–190 (PDF pp. 4–5). Naive: “The simplest case is to assume that there is no dependence across observations whatsoever in the data, which is the assumption for non-clustered RSEs: if $i \ne i'$, $j \ne j'$, **or** $t \ne t'$, then $\mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}u_{i'j't'}] = 0$, or that the errors are uncorrelated.” (Table 2; ‘or’ is bold in the paper). Repeated dyad: “The most common approach is clustering by dyad, where it is assumed that errors are correlated when $i = i'$ and $j = j'$, regardless of time period.” and “all observations in the matrix of model errors that do not share both members of the dyad are still assumed to be uncorrelated (i.e., $\mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}u_{i'j't'}] = 0$).” (Table 3). Dyadic: “By contrast, our approach only assumes independence when country pairs share no members.” and “In the matrix shown in Table 4—full dyadic clustering—we can now see that the only observations assumed to be independent are those for which the dyad does not share any members with other observations.” Tables 2–4 (p. 190) display the three patterns for six observations labelled $ijt = 111, 112, 211, 212, 221, 222$, with entries $\mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}u_{i'j't'}]$ or 0: Table 2 is diagonal; Table 3 has the three blocks $\{111,112\}$, $\{211,212\}$, $\{221,222\}$; Table 4 is zero only between $\{111,112\}$ and $\{221,222\}$.
(S4) Decomposition and DCRSEs, pp. 190–191 (PDF pp. 5–6): the display $\hat V_r = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat V_{c,i} - \hat V_D - (N-2)\hat V_0$, the sentence defining its four terms and footnotes 2 and 3 are quoted in full in P032-T11.
(S5) Reanalysis conventions, p. 192 (PDF p. 7), the last sentence running onto p. 193: “For the purposes of our reanalysis, dyads are assumed to be undirected, as modeling dyadic clustering based on directed dyads would require a stronger assumption about independence across observations.$^{11}$ Also, for the purposes of our primary reanalysis, there are no small-sample corrections made to our standard error estimates.” $N$ is not defined beside the display on p. 191; the note to Supplementary Table A.5 (supplement p. A5) says: “$N$ is the number of unique dyad members in the analytic sample.”
(S6) Terms. p. 187 (PDF p. 2): “non-incident dyads (i.e., dyads that do not share a common member)”; two observations are called incident here when their dyads share a member. KEV, p. 192: “KEVs are defined as independent variables whose parameter estimates are directly referenced in the study, or otherwise clearly pertain to the study’s stated hypotheses.” SER, p. 193 (PDF p. 8): “We compute a standard error ratio (SER) for all KEVs, which is the DCRSE divided by the standard error produced using the original variance estimation strategy.” ISFW, p. 193 and footnote 14: “where “study frequency” is the total number of KEVs for a given study appearing in the analytic sample” and “ISFW is equivalent to an average of averages across studies.”
(S7) Not in the paper. The targets index observations (records) by a single index $r$ with an unordered dyad $d_r$ of two distinct members, write $z_r$ for the bread-premultiplied score of record $r$, and call a sandwich ‘unadjusted’ when it carries no finite-sample factor. These conventions are the validators’ and are flagged where used. Every target is an exact finite statement; the two limits quoted in P032-T1 are consequences of exact identities stated there.
(S8) Which findings are targets. Of the sixteen findings rated error, five have a mathematical statement to correct or rest on an exact formal counterexample: P032-E001 (Moderate; the direction of the effect of dependence between non-incident dyads), P032-N004 (Moderate; the matrix subtracted in the decomposition for survival data), P032-E005 (Minor; the positive-semidefinite option), P032-N012 (Minor; finite-sample factors applied to Rubin-pooled matrices) and P032-E002 (Minor; a count against Supplementary Table A.2, for which the validator’s evidence is itself a Lean proof). The other eleven are not targets because their corrections change no mathematical statement: P032-E004 (an unreachable branch of the Stata command), P032-E006 (row alignment and dyad labels in the R package), P032-E008 (a selector typo that drops two KEVs; 693 for 691), P032-E009 (Supplementary Table A.3 built from the wrong result files), P032-E010 (the description of point area in Figure 3), P032-E011 (the small-sample rerun of the original standard errors), P032-N006 (the classification of Shelef 2016 as having fixed effects for both dyad members), P032-N010 (minimum Stata version), P032-N011 (an observation count in Supplementary Table A.1), P032-E003 (a cross-reference) and P032-E012 (a reference year). Of the eleven headline claims, P032-H7 (the decomposition identity), P032-H9 (the toy-example variance) and P032-H10 (the lower-bound claim, refuted by P032-E001) contain a mathematical statement; the others are empirical estimates, counts or interpretive remarks.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The Schneider and Tobin (2020) calls of the replication code (dcr with the prefix ‘mi estimate, post:’ and dofundo(asylike)): exact five-imputation, 24-observation intercept-only logit example in which removing the finite-sample factors from Rubin-pooled matrices does not give the Rubin-pooled DCR variance (the validator’s construction; not in the paper)
canonical_claim.location: Code only (no passage of main.pdf): code/1_reanalysis_stata.do lines 1312 and 1373–1385; dcr.ado lines 125–238; the results enter Supplementary Table A.2 (supplement p. A3), row Schneider and Tobin (2020). The decomposition used is the display on p. 191 (PDF p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement:
Data. Members $\{1,2,3,4\}$ ($K = 4$); the six dyads $12, 13, 14, 23, 24, 34$ with four observations each ($n = 24$); $M = 5$ completed data sets of a binary outcome. Within each dyad the outcome is 1 for the first $k$ observations and 0 for the rest, with $k = (4,2,2,2,2,0)$ for the six dyads in completion A (imputations 1–3) and $k = (4,3,3,3,3,2)$ in completion B (imputations 4–5). An intercept-only logit is fitted in each completed data set.
(a) [Fits] Completion A: $p_A = 1/2$, estimate $b_A = 0$, information $H_A = 24p_A(1-p_A) = 6$. Completion B: $p_B = 3/4$, $b_B = \log3$, $H_B = 9/2$. The scores are $s_r = y_r - p$.
(b) [Components without finite-sample factors, $U = H^{-2}\sum_{\text{clusters}}\big(\sum_{r\in\text{cluster}}s_r\big)^2$] Repeated dyad ($G_D = 6$ clusters): $U_D^A = 2/9$, $U_D^B = 8/81$. Record level ($n = 24$ clusters): $U_0^A = 1/6$, $U_0^B = 2/9$. Member $i$ (one cluster of the 12 incident observations and 12 singletons, $G_i = 13$): $U_{c,i}^A = 7/36$ for $i = 1,\ldots,4$; $U_{c,1}^B = U_{c,2}^B = 5/27$ and $U_{c,3}^B = U_{c,4}^B = 11/81$.
(c) [Completed-data DCR variances] $V_A = 4\cdot\tfrac{7}{36} - \tfrac29 - 2\cdot\tfrac16 = \tfrac29$ and $V_B = 2\cdot\tfrac{5}{27} + 2\cdot\tfrac{11}{81} - \tfrac{8}{81} - 2\cdot\tfrac29 = \tfrac{8}{81}$, each equal to the direct sum over pairs of observations sharing a member; their average over the five imputations is $\bar V = \tfrac{14}{81}$.
(d) [Rubin’s between-imputation term] The five estimates are $(0,0,0,L,L)$ with $L = \log3$, so $\bar b = 2L/5$, $B = \tfrac{3}{10}L^2$ and $Q = (1+\tfrac1M)B = \tfrac{9}{25}L^2$.
(e) [DCR within each imputation, then Rubin pooling] $T_* = \bar V + Q = \tfrac{14}{81} + \tfrac{9}{25}\log^23$.
(f) [What the code computes] Each component is first pooled with its software finite-sample factor, $T_j = \bar U_j/a_j + Q$, where $\bar U_j$ is the average of the component over the five imputations and $a_D = 1 - 1/G_D = 5/6$, $a_0 = 1 - 1/n = 23/24$, $a_i = 1 - 1/G_i = 12/13$; the code then forms $T_{code} = \sum_{i=1}^4a_iT_i - a_DT_D - (K-2)a_0T_0$. Here $$T_{code} = \tfrac{14}{81} + c\,Q,\qquad c = 4\cdot\tfrac{12}{13} - \tfrac56 - 2\cdot\tfrac{23}{24} = \tfrac{49}{52},$$ so $T_{code} = \tfrac{14}{81} + \tfrac{441}{1300}\log^23$ and $$T_{code} - T_* = (c-1)Q = -\tfrac{27}{1300}\log^23 < 0.$$
All completed-data DCR variances and both pooled variances are positive, so the eigenvalue step of footnote 3 is inactive.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Decomposition: P032-T11 and P032-T4 (i); $K$ is the number of distinct dyad members (the paper’s $N$; the validator writes $K$ to keep it apart from the observation count $n$). For an intercept-only binary logit the fitted probability is the sample mean $p$, the estimate is $\log(p/(1-p))$, the score of an observation is $y_r - p$ and the information is $np(1-p)$. Rubin’s rules for $M$ imputations with estimates $b_m$ and within-imputation variances $W_m$: $\bar b = M^{-1}\sum_mb_m$, $B = (M-1)^{-1}\sum_m(b_m - \bar b)(b_m - \bar b)^T$, total variance $M^{-1}\sum_mW_m + (1+1/M)B$. As recorded by the validator from the staged code: the three calls at lines 1375, 1380 and 1385 of 1_reanalysis_stata.do pass `dm1(cc) dm2(dc) crse(donor_country) psd dofundo(asylike) syntax(vce)` and `prefix(mi estimate, post:)`, after `add(5)` imputations at line 1312; dcr.ado reads each component’s e(V) after the prefix has pooled it and multiplies the whole matrix by the undo factor $(G-1)/G$ or $(n-1)/n$ (lines 153–157, 163–190, 199–238). With one fitted parameter the software’s completed-data factors $G/(G-1)$ and $n/(n-1)$ are the reciprocals of these $a_j$.
canonical_claim.note: P032-N012 is rated an error, Minor: a finding about the code path of one study (three models, 18 KEVs) with no corresponding statement in the article, included because it rests on an exact formal counterexample and an exact general identity (P032-T9). Every value in (a)–(f) was recomputed exactly when this list was fixed, the completed-data DCR variances both from the decomposition and from the direct sum over pairs. Not established: any numerical error, its sign or its size in the Schneider and Tobin row of Table A.2; Stata was not run. The complete data set is in the artifact (counterexample_data.csv).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 4.1 (p. 196), ‘Three studies see half or more of their KEVs become insignificant at the 5% level upon reanalysis’, corrected against Supplementary Table A.2: four studies have a Sig.→Insig. share of one half or more, and three have a share above one half
canonical_claim.location: p. 196 (PDF p. 11), Section 4.1, paragraph beginning ‘For individual studies’; Supplementary Table A.2 (supplement p. A3), columns KEVs, Sig.→Insig. and Avg. SER
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed (p. 196): “For individual studies, the average SER ranges from 0.90 to 4.16, as seen in Supplementary Table A.2. On average, KEVs from 18 of 22 studies are less precise after accounting for dyadic clustering. Only 7 of 22 studies do not lose statistical significance in any KEV estimates due to DCRSE re-estimation. Three studies see half or more of their KEVs become insignificant at the 5% level upon reanalysis.”
Sol’s smallest repair (validated.json, P032-E002), verbatim: “Replace 'Three' with 'Four' in the sentence on p. 196. Alternatively, retaining 'Three' and replacing 'half or more' with 'more than half' produces a correct strict-threshold description. Replace 'defering' with 'deferring' in the Efrat–Newman and Pratt topic descriptions in Table A.2.”
Data (Supplementary Table A.2, ‘Primary Results, Study Level’, the 22 study rows in printed order; for each study the number of KEVs $n_i$, the printed Sig.→Insig. proportion $r_i$ and the printed Avg. SER). Arel-Bundock (2017): 6, 0.167, 2.739; Bermeo (2017): 173, 0.249, 2.187; Bermeo and Leblang (2015): 29, 0.207, 2.2; Carter and Poast (2020): 8, 0.375, 1.099; Colgan (2014): 9, 0.889, 3.269; Colgan and Weeks (2015): 24, 0, 1.526; Copelovitch and Putnam (2014): 45, 0.111, 0.898; Dietrich (2016): 36, 0.139, 1.511; Efrat and Newman (2016): 4, 0.5, 4.158; Fang, Johnson, and Leeds (2014): 1, 1, 1.691; Goemans and Schultz (2017): 170, 0.041, 0.955; Horowitz and Stam (2014): 3, 0, 1.895; Kinne (2018): 6, 0, 1.301; McDonald (2015): 41, 0.195, 1.432; Powell (2015): 16, 0, 0.908; Pratt (2018): 18, 0.222, 1.426; Renshon (2016): 20, 0.05, 1.291; Schneider and Tobin (2020): 18, 0, 0.999; Shelef (2016): 9, 0, 1.071; Sommerer and Tallberg (2019): 15, 0, 1.212; Weisiger (2016): 28, 0.607, 3.268; Weisiger and Yarhi-Milo (2015): 12, 0.167, 1.311.
Formal content (exact arithmetic on the printed table).
(i) [Integer counts] Each proportion is $k_i/n_i$ for an integer $0\le k_i\le n_i$ (a mean of 0/1 indicators over the study’s $n_i$ KEVs, printed to three decimals). In every row exactly one integer $k_i$ satisfies $|k_i/n_i - r_i|\le\tfrac{1}{2000}$; in table order, $k = (1, 43, 6, 3, 8, 0, 5, 5, 2, 1, 7, 0, 0, 8, 0, 4, 1, 0, 0, 0, 17, 2)$.
(ii) [Half or more] $2k_i\ge n_i$ holds for exactly four rows: Colgan (2014), $8/9$; Efrat and Newman (2016), $2/4$; Fang, Johnson, and Leeds (2014), $1/1$; Weisiger (2016), $17/28$. The number of studies with a share of one half or more is therefore 4, not 3. The same four rows are the ones with printed $r_i\ge0.5$.
(iii) [More than half] $2k_i > n_i$ holds for exactly three rows: the four of (ii) without Efrat and Newman (2016), whose share is exactly $2/4 = 1/2$.
(iv) [The neighbouring counts are right] There are 22 rows; $\sum_in_i = 691$; exactly 7 rows have $k_i = 0$; exactly 18 rows have Avg. SER above 1; the smallest and largest Avg. SER are 0.898 and 4.158.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: KEV, SER: (S6). Significance is at the 5% level (p. 193: “estimates that lose statistical significance at a conventional level (i.e., 5%)”). ‘Sig.→Insig.’ in Table A.2 is the share of a study’s KEVs whose $p$-value is significant with the original standard error and insignificant with the DCRSE; the denominator is all of the study’s KEVs (the four transition columns of each row sum to 1 up to rounding). ‘Half or more’ is read as a share $\ge1/2$. That each printed proportion is a mean of 0/1 indicators rounded to three decimals is the validator’s reading of code/3_reanalysis_merge.R, lines 488–505. The table values were read from the page image of supplement p. A3.
canonical_claim.note: P032-E002 is rated an error, Minor: a descriptive count off by one; the table beside the sentence shows the right figures and nothing rests on the count. It is a finding about reporting and is a target because it rests on exact arithmetic on the printed table: the validator’s evidence is itself a Lean proof of (ii)–(iv) for the pairs $(n_i,k_i)$ (check.lean in the artifact, compiled with no sorry; the count of rows with Avg. SER above 1 and the range are not in that file). The formalizer may reuse or restate it. The unique-integer recovery in (i) and every count in (ii)–(iv) were recomputed when this list was fixed. The second part of the finding (‘defering’ for ‘deferring’ in two labels of Table A.2) is a spelling matter and not a target.
